flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Test your retention of core constitutional concepts and comparisons.

items.question: Does an unwritten constitution mean that none of its principles are written down?
items.answer: No. An unwritten constitution contains many written laws (e.g., UK's Bill of Rights, Magna Carta), but it is 'unwritten' because those laws are not codified in a single, supreme document.

items.question: What is the primary factor that makes a constitution 'rigid'?
items.answer: A constitution is rigid if it requires a special, complex procedure for its amendment (like the US, which requires 2/3 of Congress and 3/4 of states), making it harder to change than ordinary laws.

items.question: Which system of government features Parliamentary Supremacy, and how does it relate to its constitution?
items.answer: The United Kingdom features Parliamentary Supremacy. Because its constitution is unwritten and flexible, Parliament can amend any constitutional principle through a simple majority vote (ordinary lawmaking).

items.question: How is the amendment procedure of the Indian Constitution a compromise between rigidity and flexibility?
items.answer: It provides three routes: some amendments require a simple majority (flexible), others a special majority under Article 368 (rigid), and federal provisions require a special majority plus ratification by half of the states (highly rigid).

traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Trap 1: Confusing the UK's 'flexible' constitution with complete instability. Even though the UK constitution is flexible, robust conventions and democratic traditions prevent sudden, authoritarian changes.

Trap 2: Assuming all amendments in India fall under Article 368. Amendments made by simple majority (like creating new states or altering legislative councils) are explicitly deemed not to be amendments under Article 368.

Trap 3: Claiming judicial review is equally powerful everywhere. In a country with a written constitution and judicial supremacy (like the US), courts can strike down laws easily. In the UK (parliamentary supremacy), courts cannot override Acts of Parliament.

sections.title: 1. Written vs. Unwritten & Rigid vs. Flexible Constitutions
sections.content:
Constitutions are structural frameworks that establish the rules of governance for a state. The primary methods of classifying them are based on their codification (Written vs. Unwritten) and their ease of amendment (Rigid vs. Flexible).

Written Constitutions

A written constitution is a single, codified document drafted by a representative body (like a Constituent Assembly) at a specific historical point. It establishes constitutional supremacy, meaning the constitution is the highest law of the land, and all other laws must conform to it. Examples: USA, India.

Unwritten Constitutions

An unwritten constitution is not codified in a single book. Instead, it is a cumulative body of constitutional conventions, judicial precedents, and key legislative acts passed over centuries. It features parliamentary supremacy, meaning parliament can pass any law to alter the constitution. Example: United Kingdom.

Rigid Constitutions

A constitution is rigid if it distinguishes between constitutional law and ordinary law, requiring a complex, special process to amend it. For example, the US Constitution requires a two-thirds vote in both Houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states. This ensures structural stability.

Flexible Constitutions

A flexible constitution makes no distinction between constitutional and ordinary laws. Both can be enacted, amended, or repealed using the exact same simple legislative process. This allows the state to quickly adapt its basic framework to societal changes. Example: UK.

sections.title: 2. Federal vs. Unitary Divisions and India's Unique Synthesis
sections.content:
Another vital classification is the distribution of power between the center and regional units: Federal vs. Unitary. Additionally, some constitutions are classified based on their origin (Enacted vs. Evolved).

Federal Constitutions

A federal constitution divides powers between a central government and state/provincial governments. Both levels derive power directly from the constitution, which acts as the supreme referee. It requires a rigid constitution and an independent judiciary to resolve disputes. Examples: USA, Canada.

Unitary Constitutions

In a unitary constitution, all governing powers are concentrated in the national government. Regional bodies may exist, but they are subordinate entities whose authority is delegated and can be revoked by the center. A written constitution is not strictly required. Examples: UK, France.

The Indian Constitution: A Unique Synthesis

The framers of the Indian Constitution avoided selecting an extreme model. Instead, they designed a unique synthesis of elements from different systems:

  • Written & Lengthiest: India chose a written constitution to manage its vast diversity, detailed administrative provisions, and fundamental rights.
  • Synthesis of Rigidity & Flexibility: Under Article 368, some clauses require a special majority (2/3 present & voting + absolute majority), while federal changes require ratification by half the states (rigid). However, several other matters can be amended via simple majority (flexible).
  • Federal Structure with a Unitary Bias: Often described as "quasi-federal" (by K.C. Wheare), India is a federal union of states with a strong centralizing character (unitary features like emergency provisions, single citizenship, and unified judiciary).
  • Synthesis of Sovereignty and Supremacy: It balances the British principle of Parliamentary Sovereignty with the American principle of Judicial Supremacy. The judiciary can declare parliamentary laws unconstitutional, but Parliament can amend major parts of the constitution to override judicial rulings (subject to the Basic Structure doctrine).

Key Differences at a Glance

Dimension Written / Codified Unwritten / Uncodified
Source of Supremacy The Constitution itself is supreme (Constitutional Supremacy). The legislature is supreme (Parliamentary Supremacy).
Role of Judiciary Wide powers of judicial review to declare laws void. Limited scope; courts interpret laws but cannot invalidate Acts.
Flexibility of Amendment Usually rigid; requires a special amendment procedure. Flexible; amended by ordinary parliamentary laws.
